claims.text: Aluminum enrichment can make a high-entropy alloy lightweight or ultralight.
Selective laser melting can be used to process high-entropy alloys.
Controlled volumetric energy density and optimized scanning strategies improve the processing of the proposed Al-enriched alloy.
The additive-manufacturing process produces finer, uniformly distributed grains.
The additive-manufacturing process produces an optimized phase distribution.
Precise control of thermal gradients and energy input during SLM promotes rapid solidification.
Rapid solidification refines the grain structure.
Rapid solidification and controlled thermal gradients tailor the alloy's phase distribution.
Grain refinement and phase tailoring reduce the overall density of the alloy.
The SLM-processed alloy will have lower density than the same alloy made by conventional processing.
The SLM-processed alloy will have greater strength than the same alloy made by conventional processing.
The SLM-processed alloy will have greater stiffness than the same alloy made by conventional processing.
The SLM-processed alloy will have greater durability than the same alloy made by conventional processing.
The proposed benefits are expected under standard ambient structural-service conditions.
Performance under high temperature, severe irradiation, or other extreme environments remains untested.

contradictions.description: The initial-state and baseline descriptions allow or imply a material without aluminum enrichment, whereas the predicted outcome invokes the same alloy and the experiment explicitly uses the same Al-enriched composition in both processing groups.

The hypothesis intervention combines aluminum enrichment with optimized SLM, and the stated baseline can lack both changes, but the proposed experiment holds aluminum enrichment constant and therefore tests only the processing contribution.
